title: September 2026 Opportunities: Open Calls, Residencies, and Grants for Artists
description: Every month, we share opportunities for artists and designers, including open calls, grants, fellowships, and residencies. Make sure you never mis
body:
Every month, we share opportunities for artists and designers, including open calls, grants, fellowships, and residencies. Make sure you never miss out by joining our monthly Opportunities Newsletter.
Hayama Artist ResidencyFeaturedLaunched in 2020, the Hayama Artist Residency offers visual artists from around the world a unique opportunity to spend four weeks in Japan for rest, reflection, and creative inspiration. Selected artists receive roundtrip airfare, a private bedroom, and an $800 stipend to cover meals and local transportation. We welcome applications from visual artists working in any medium and at any stage of their career. Applicants must be at least 21 years old. The residency runs June 1 to 30, 2027, and selected artists will be notified by December 15, 2026. There is a $95 application fee. For more information and to apply, please visit www.hayamaresidency.comDeadline: September 30, 2026.
Summer $1,800 Innovate Grants for Art + PhotoFeaturedInnovate Grant awards two $1,800 grants each quarter to one visual artist and one photographer. In addition, 18 applicants will receive honorable mentions, be featured on the website, and join a growing community. International artists and photographers working in any medium are eligible. All applicants retain the right to the work they submit.Deadline: 11:59 p.m. PDT on September 17, 2026.
Open Calls
Hunt Museum Open Submission Exhibition (International)The Hunt Open Submission Exhibition is an initiative celebrating contemporary Irish and international art at the Hunt Museum in Limerick. There is a €15 entry fee for the first image, plus an additional €15 per artwork for up to three submissions.Deadline: September 7, 2026.
CraftForms 2026 Open Call(International)Wayne Art Center seeks submissions for CraftForms 2026, the 31st International Juried Exhibition of Contemporary Fine Craft, in the following mediums: basketry, ceramics, fiber, furniture, glass, jewelry, metal, mixed media, paper, wearable art, and wood. Works created utilizing CAD/CAM technologies and 3D printing tools are also eligible. Selected works will be on display in from December 5, 2026, through January 23, 2027. This year’s Jurors, Dr. Robert K. Liu and Patrick Benesh-Liu, of Ornament Magazine, will present $12,000+ in prizes.Deadline: 11:59 p.m. MDT on September 8, 2026.
Bridging the Gap Open Call for Documentary Proposals(Scotland and Northern Ireland)The Scottish Documentary Institute seeks new and emerging talent based in Scotland and Northern Ireland with an idea for a short documentary. Twelve projects are shortlisted based on proposals and visual materials. Selected filmmakers will develop their ideas through intensive workshops led by international filmmakers and leading industry professionals, and four films will receive a full commission.Deadline: September 9, 2026.
Hiding in Plain Site: International Public Art Short Film Festival(International)HPS invites filmmakers, artists, and creative practitioners to submit short works between two and 20 minutes for consideration in this screening program, which will premiere on October 25 in Minneapolis. HPS seeks to bring together film, video art, experimental media, XR (extended reality), and other works that expand how public art is experienced and represented. Deadline: September 10, 2026.
Dobell Prize for Drawing(Australia)The Dobell Drawing Prize is Australia’s leading award for drawing and an unparalleled celebration of technique, innovation and expanded practice. Presented at the National Art School in partnership with the Sir William Dobell Art Foundation, this biennial exhibition continues to highlight the enduring relevance and changing role of drawing within contemporary art practices. The winner will receive an AUD$30,000 acquisitive prize, and the work enters the National Art School’s collection.Deadline: September 14, 2026.
Queering Wood Craft Open Call(International)This exhibition, presented by the Museum for Art in Wood, will highlight queer-identified makers working in wood and be both an exploration and celebration of the dynamic intersections between contemporary wood practices and the multiple meanings of “queer.” Queering Wood Craft will take place between April and July 2027.Deadline: September 15, 2026.
Queensland Regional Art Awards(Queensland)The Queensland Regional Art Awards are Flying Arts’ annual prize, open to artists living in regional, rural, and remote Queensland. This year’s total pool of AUD$326,800 spans cash awards, solo exhibitions, artist residencies, and professional development opportunities. Entry fees are $25 per entry for artists aged 15 to 25, and $40 for those over 25 ($35 for members).Deadline: September 18, 2026.
All About Photography Open Call: STREET (International)AAP Magazine wants to discover your unique vision of urban life for its street-themed issue. Submit a cohesive body of work or portfolio exploring street life in any way you choose. The publication welcomes all approaches, styles, and interpretations. Black-and-white, color, and monochromatic treatments are all welcome. There is an application fee of $35 for three images, or $30 if submitted before the early bird deadline.Deadline: September 29, 2026 (early bird deadline is September 8).
Global Lens Photography Awards(International)The Global Lens Awards recognizes remarkable visual authorship across categories including advertising, architecture, black-and-white, nature, and fine art. Selected photographers receive recognition designed to extend beyond the results announcement, including certificates, publication in an annual book, virtual exhibition placement. The top winner receives a €1,000 cash prize, trophy, and prominent exhibition placement.Deadline: September 30, 2026.
Field Notes from the Middle: Call for Midwest Photographic Artists(Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Dakota, Ohio, South Dakota, Wisconsin)Filter Photo invites photographers making work about the Midwest to submit to Field Notes from the Middle, an inaugural juried exhibition. This call is open to photography, photographic materials, and other lens-based artwork that engages with the region. Juror Nathaniel M. Stein, Curator of Photography at the Cincinnati Art Museum, will select five artists to each exhibit images from a single body of work. Each of the exhibiting artists will be eligible for the 2026 Filter Photo Museum Purchase Award of $2,000, with the selected work acquired by the Cincinnati Art Museum for its permanent collection.Deadline: September 30, 2026.
YICCA Art Prize(International)This competition is open to all media and techniques and geared toward emerging artists, with a total prize pool of €5,500. The application fee varies depending on the number of images submitted and starts at €50.Deadline: October 8, 2026.
Arch Enemy Arts Call for Artists(International)Arch Enemy Arts is seeking submissions for an annual group exhibition in January 2027. This spotlight exhibition of new and emerging talent has no themes or direction in subject matter, although the gallery focuses on representational, dark surrealism, magical realism, post-graffiti, pop-surrealism, narrative, illustrative, and figurative work across a range of artistic mediums. The exhibition is open to artists worldwide, who are invited to submit up to three works for consideration.Deadline: 11:59 p.m. EST on November 13, 2026.
Grants
Henry Moore Institute Travel & Research Grants(International)These grants of up to £2,500 are available to sculpture historians, academics, and conservators who are researching and publishing on sculpture conservation, production, history and/or interpretation, to support research costs, travel, photography and archival access.Deadline: September 1, 2026.
Dezi Art Prize(International)This global juried art grant is geared toward emerging and early-career visual artists. Two winners each receive a $1,000 unrestricted grant, plus a featured profile. Ten finalists are named and featured. Open worldwide, all visual media is welcome, with entries scored on merit by an independent jury. There is a $30 application fee.Deadline: September 10, 2026.
2026-27 MCAD-Jerome Foundation Fellowship for Early Career Artists(Minnesota)Artists considered for the MCAD-Jerome Foundation Fellowship may work in a variety of visual art media, including traditional and new media. The program is aimed at visual artists who can present their work in a gallery context. Eligible applicants must be in the early stages of their careers and have not yet attained professional acknowledgment commensurate with the quality of their work. An independent jury of three arts professionals awards four grants of $10,000 each to early-career Minnesota artists.Deadline: 12 p.m. CDT on September 11, 2026.
The 1858 Prize for Contemporary Southern Art(U.S. South)The Gibbes Museum and Society 1858’s Prize for Contemporary Southern Art awards $10,000 to an artist whose work contributes to a new understanding of art in the South. Presented annually, the prize recognizes the highest level of artistic achievement and welcomes applications from artist working across any media. Artists who reside, work in, or are from Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Virginia, and West Virginia are encouraged and eligible to apply. There is a $35 application fee.Deadline: September 14, 2026.
Rauschenberg Medical Emergency Grants(International)The Rauschenberg Medical Emergency Grants program provides one-time grants of up to $5,000 for recent unexpected medical, dental, and mental health emergencies to artists in financial need who are creating work in the visual arts, digital/electronic arts, video/film, and choreography.Deadline: 5 p.m. EDT on September 15, 2026.
2027-28 QM-Jerome Foundation Fellowship for Emerging Artists(New York City)The Queens Museum (QM) launches its eighth iteration of the QM-Jerome Foundation Fellowship for Emerging Artists in New York City. Two visual artists will receive $20,000 each and professional development consultations from QM staff members working toward an artist’s project. Each fellow will also receive mentorship from a New York-based established artist. The fellowships will culminate in solo project exhibitions at the Queens Museum in 2028. The duration of each fellowship is one year, culminating with the opening of the fellow’s exhibition.Deadline: 11:59 p.m. EDT on September 28, 2026.
Tom Stoddard Award for Excellence x GOST Books(International)This unique award offers established photographers working in long-form documentary photography a photo book produced by world renowned publisher GOST Books. The winner will also receive £5,000 toward expenses, travel to see printing in Verona, and publicity in The Guardian. There is a £50 fee per entry.Deadline: 11:59 p.m. BST on September 30, 2026.
The Supporting Act Foundation Artist Grants(Europe)The Supporting Act Foundation offers 10 unrestricted grants of €10,000 each, paid in monthly installments of €1,000. The program aims to improve living conditions for artists, enabling them to dedicate more time to developing their practices. To be eligible, artists must be based in Belgium, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, or the U.K.Deadline: October 1, 2026.
The Adolf and Esther Gottlieb Emergency Grant (International)This program provides one-time financial assistance to qualified painters, printmakers, and sculptors whose needs resulted from an unforeseen catastrophic incident and who lack the resources to meet that situation. Awardees typically receive $5,000 and up to $15,000.Deadline: Rolling.
Pollock-Krasner Foundation Grant (International)The foundation welcomes applications from painters, sculptors, and artists working on paper, including printmakers. Grants are intended for one year and range up to $50,000. The artist’s circumstances determine the size of the grant, and professional exhibition history will be considered.Deadline: Rolling.
Residencies, Fellowships, & More
Surel’s Place Month-Long Residencies(International)Surel’s Place supports artists by providing time, shelter, and professional support your work deserves. In exchange, the organization asks you to offer art experiences to the community in Garden City, Idaho. Residents receive free housing and studio space, a $100 stipend per week, a $300 travel stipend, and more. This open call is for residences that occur between January and May 2027.Deadline: September 1, 2026.
Kimmel Harding Nelson Center for the Arts Residencies(International)The mission of the Kimmel Harding Nelson Center for the Arts in Nebraska City is to support artists by providing working and living environments that allow uninterrupted time for work, reflection, and creative growth. Residency applications are currently open for composers, musicians, interdisciplinary artists, visual artists, writers, and poets. There is a $35 application fee.Deadline: September 1, 2026.
2027 National Gallery of Iceland Residency(International)The National Gallery of Iceland is seeking applications to its CUSP program, a European cooperation project funded through Creative Europe’s Culture grant. Artists working in complex media or emerging technologies are invited to apply. The residency will be up to four weeks long, and accommodation, workspace, and stipends are provided.Deadline: 11:59 p.m. GMT on September 2, 2026.
ON::View Artist Residency Program(International)Located in the heart of Savannah’s Starland District at ARTS Southeast, the fully-funded ON::View Artist Residency provides a free, high-visibility studio space, lodging, and a $500 stipend for an artist or curator to complete a new project, continue an in-progress endeavor, or to conduct research. There is a $50 application fee.Deadline: 11:59 p.m. ET on September 7, 2026.
MacDowell Fellowships for Spring/Summer 2027(International)Located in Peterborough, New Hampshire, MacDowell encourages applications from artists of all backgrounds and all countries in the following disciplines: architecture, film/video, interdisciplinary arts, literature, music composition, theatre, and visual arts. A fellowship consists of exclusive use of a private studio, accommodations, and three prepared meals a day for two to eight weeks.Deadline: September 10, 2026.
Art Omi: Artists Residencies(International)The Art Omi: Artists residency invites practitioners from all over the world, representing a wide diversity of artistic styles and practices, to gather, collaborate, and share ideas. Concentrated time for studio work is balanced with cultural exchange and critical appraisal, fostering deep creative and professional connections in a lively social setting. There is a $15 application fee.Deadline: September 14, 2026.
Art Omi Dance, Music, and Architecture Residencies(International)Art Omi: Architecture nurtures experimentation in environs that offer a singular blend of rural quiet and cultural stimulation. Residents present their work to the public during the Open Studios event at the end of the residency period. Art Omi: Dance brings together accomplished dance artists from around the world. Residents experience each other’s creative process and the freedom to play in this collaborative residency program. And Art Omi: Music welcomes musicians, composers, and sound-makers working in all genres and hailing from around the globe for a uniquely collaborative music-making residency. There is a $15 application fee for each.Deadline: October 1, 2026.
Glen Arbor Arts Center Residency(International)The Glen Arbor Arts Center offers several opportunities for artist residencies each year. The purpose of the residency program is to provide visiting artists with a respite from daily responsibilities to enable them to concentrate on their work. Housing and studio space are provided for each two-week residency, and artists may work in disciplines of creative writing, visual art, photography, sculpture, fiber arts, ceramics, and music. There is a $35 application fee.Deadline: 2 p.m. EDT on November 5, 2026.
INDENT Emerging Filmmaker Opportunities(U.S.)INDENT, a Pittsburgh nonprofit, hires emerging filmmakers into paid, full-time roles on professional independent productions. Five paid opportunities are open now. Two are post-production roles on an original, Pittsburgh-rooted feature documentary, running mid-December 2026 through mid-March 2027. Three are full-production roles on a short-form nonfiction episodic series, working across development, production, and post, running mid-January through mid-April 2027. Each placement is a twelve-week position with a $10,000 stipend, direct mentorship from working professionals, and a finished production credit. Filmmakers must be able to relocate to Pittsburgh for the placement.Deadline: Rolling/Until filled.
Quarantine (International)Dubbed “purgatory for artists,” Quarantine is a week-long intensive art program on an 18th-century quarantine island off the coast of Menorca, Spain. The program is open to beginners and professionals alike and offers three 45-minute private mentorships throughout the week, with activities lasting 12+ hours per day. Phones are banned.Deadline: Rolling.
Residencia Corazón (International)Residencia Corazón is an independent, artist-run residency in LaPlata, Argentina—a home for artists since 2006. The program welcomes visualartists, writers, curators, and creative researchers from around theworld for one- to three-month residencies. Each stay is fully personalized, and fees range from $800 to $1,500 per month.Deadline: Rolling.

title: Thieves Snatch $4.6M Diamond Necklace From Viennese Museum
description:
News
                The two thieves paid entry before stealing the 673- white diamond necklace that once belonged to Queen Nazl
body:
News
                The two thieves paid entry before stealing the 673- white diamond necklace that once belonged to Queen Nazli of Egypt.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            An exhibition view of GLANZSTÜCKE: Van Cleef & Arpels High Jewelry × Masterpieces from the MAK Collection (2026) shows the necklace that was stolen from the museum. (© Van Cleef & Arpels; courtesy Museum of Applied Arts, Vienna)
    
        
            Two visitors smashed a display case and made off with a platinum and diamond necklace at the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK) in Vienna yesterday afternoon, August 27. Per the Viennese daily newspaper Der Standard, the Van Cleef & Arpels necklace was last appraised at $4.6 million by Sotheby's. It was displayed as part of Glanzstücke, an ongoing exhibition featuring over 500 works gathered from the museum's design collection and the French luxury jewelry house. The 200-karat, 673-white diamond necklace was designed in 1939 for Egyptian Queen Nazli on the occasion of her daughter Princess Fawzia's marriage to Iranian Prince Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, who later became Iran's last shah.A press statement from the museum confirmed the theft, but officials declined to comment further due to the ongoing investigation. Austrian media outlets reported that the two men paid for their ticketed entry into the museum before approaching the display case containing the necklace, a set of earrings, and a double-clip brooch from the same collection, along with two decorative wares.

title: Demolition of Georgian Architectural Landmark Sparks Outcry
description:
News
                Civilians, architects, and members of the preservationist community are advocating to save the complex know
body:
News
                Civilians, architects, and members of the preservationist community are advocating to save the complex known locally as the Rike Tubes in the capital city Tbilisi.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Rike Park Music Theatre and Exhibition Hall in Tbilisi, Georgia (Courtesy Levan Davlianidze via Wikimedia Commons, CC-BY-4.0)
    
        
            Demolitions are underway on the Rike Park Music Theatre and Exhibition Hall in Tbilisi, Georgia, prompting outcry from local community members and the architects who designed the two-structure complex. Set against the historic 19th-century buildings that define the capital city's dominant style, the landmark is known as the “Rike Tubes” for its futuristic appearance, a reminder of the country’s modernist push from the 2000s to the early 2010s.The Tbilisi City Hall’s Architectural Service issued the demolition permit in June to the owner, Rike Dom, with the dismantling process commencing last month and due to wrap up by December. In interviews with Reuters and local outlets, many expressed concerns with the decision, describing the tourist hotspot as a defining feature of the capital city skyline.Italian architects Massimiliano and Doriana Fuksas, of Fuksas Studio, were asked to design the complex for musical performance and contemporary art exhibitions in 2010, under then-Prime Minister Nika Gilauri and United National Movement (UNM) President Mikheil Saakashvili (who has been in prison for nearly five years for abuse of power charges). Construction began on the glass-and-steel tubes in 2011. When the conservative Georgian Dream party came into power in 2012, officials froze construction, leaving the project unfinished.

title: The Belgian Exhibition That Strives to "Decenter" the West
description:
Art Review
                With two contradictory briefs — to both decenter Europe and show Bruges’s centrality in international
body:
Art Review
                With two contradictory briefs — to both decenter Europe and show Bruges’s centrality in international networks — an exhibition on the Belgian city is already off to a bumpy start.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Installation view of Jan van Eyck, "Portret van Margareta van Eyck" (1439) in Bigger Picture: Connected worlds of Bruges 900-1550 at BRUSK (© Jan Darthet; all images courtesy BRUSK)
    
        
            BRUGES, Belgium — With its cobblestone streets, glossy green canals, and stepped gable townhouses, Bruges has the self-contained and unchanging quality of a scene in a snow globe. Bigger Picture: Connected worlds of Bruges 900-1550 seeks to bust this myth, demonstrating the extent of the city’s historical connection with the rest of the world. The inaugural exhibition of BRUSK — “BRU” for Bruges and “SK” for schone kunsten (“fine art”) — a large new gallery attached to the Groeningemuseum, the show is guest curated by Peter Frankopan, an Oxford medievalist and author of a popular history of the Silk Road. In addition to demonstrating Bruges’s global connections, the exhibition also invokes the notion of decentering the “West” from its self-appointed position as the hub of civilization, via a video presentation, starring Frankopan, that plays at its entry. With these two somewhat contradictory briefs — to both decenter Europe and show Bruges’s centrality in international networks — the exhibition is off to a bumpy start. A further complication is the vast number and type of objects on display: There are over 250 items, ranging from a surprisingly covetable chain mail jacket and underwhelming shreds of ancient silk to significant paintings by Titian, Jan van Eyck, and Hans Memling, as well as religious relics, manuscripts of North African and European origin, Turkish carpets, Viking artifacts, coins, religious garb, and more.Installation view of Bigger Picture: Connected worlds of Bruges 900-1550(© Stad Brugge)To manage this vast range of materials, the exhibition is divided into four “worlds,” each defined by its own intricately designed enclosure delimited by hanging cloth. The “North Sea World,” for instance, is made up of triangular panels that recall sails, while the “Mediterranean World” is under a pavilion-style tent. Each world also has a distinct soundscape — the Mediterranean is evoked by a twitter of birds and the sound of creaking wagon wheels. “The World of Christianity” has bells and more birds. The “World of the Court” is accompanied, like a medieval feast, by gentle plucking on string instruments. In the darkened gallery, the worlds form dramatically lit islands, linked by white lines painted on the floor. Aided by the inventive but not illuminating animations playing in each world, the whole installation is reminiscent of the opening credits for Game of Thrones.
                  
                      
                        Art Review
                      
                      
                        Belgium

title: A View From the Easel
description:
Community
                “It's just me, my dogs, and my turtle.”
body:
Community
                “It's just me, my dogs, and my turtle.”
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            Welcome to the 352nd installment of A View From the Easel, a series in which artists reflect on their workspace. This week, printmaker and self-proclaimed "mountain ultrarunner" Hilary Lorenz transforms paper into boats, books, and weavings in the studio she built herself.Want to take part? Check out our submission guidelines and share a bit about your studio with us through this form! All mediums and workspaces are welcome, including your home studio.Hilary Lorenz, Abiquiu, New MexicoHow long have you been working in this space?I have been officially in my studio on and off since 2013. I bought a small house in rural New Mexico in 2010 and started building my studio the following summer. I was still living in NYC and spending three months a year in Abiquiu until I moved here in 2022. I am actually in Medanales, but many of us have multiple addresses for the post office, utility, etc. So it can be confusing. I built my studio with the help of two neighbors; it is entirely out of stones I picked up off a mountain, mud, local timber, and windows from Habitat for Humanity Restore.Describe an average day in your studio.I did not run electricity lines to my studio, which I didn’t think I needed since I work during the day in natural light. Not having electricity or Wi-Fi keeps me from getting lost on the internet. After I walk my dogs at 7am, I then run for an hour or so. I fill my water bottle and enter the studio. I normally work on one or two pieces at a time, so I look at what I completed the day before, evaluate my materials (always paper), and begin working. Studio time is almost always production time; I am producing physical artwork. I save my digital admin stuff to midday. In the summer it gets so hot, in the high 90s, that it is miserable to work in the studio from about 2pm to 6 pm; that is when I go into the house, which is cool, to do any grant writing or exhibition planning, anything that needs communication. After it cools off, I go back out to the studio for one to two hours. My studio is about 100 meters from the house.How does the space affect your work?I love what I built. My studio is a place of comfort and security. When I am working at my 10-foot table, I look out my open glass doors to the mountains. I attached a corral to my studio for the dogs to hang out, and there is an acre they can wander around in. I often sit outside when I need to clear my head. But the outdoors also offers me additional space to do big messy projects, like my linocut-printed paper canoe or my "Shipwrecked" installation piece.How do you interact with the environment outside your studio?I am always looking outside when I am working. I set myself up so that when I am weaving my prints and drawings together, I can see outside. I also have three entrances to the studio and a lot of windows so that I can have the feeling of being in a protected space, protected from the sun and wind, but also feel like I am outside. I am also a mountain ultrarunner, so I spend huge amounts of time outdoors and in the mountains. It is an integral part of my making process. But being so rural, unless I leave there, it's just me, my dogs, and my turtle. It is rare to see people, which can be unsettling.What do you love about your studio?I am incredibly proud that I built it, and I hauled five massive truckloads of rocks that I picked up myself off the mountain to build the walls. I love that it is mine and I don’t pay rent. I love that I built my tables, and it gives me a sense of independence. Because I live so rurally, I mostly have to do things myself, which can be a struggle, but that is the way it is. I love constantly learning how to solve whatever problems come my way. I also love that when I go away, I can lock the door and leave. The building is mud and stone; it is strong and secure and requires minimal maintenance, but it is made from earth and one day, hopefully not for a very long time, it will naturally decompose right back into the ground.What do you wish were different?The absolutely toughest part of being here is the isolation. I am not fond of isolation. I am happy to be alone and work alone, but then I want to be able to walk out my door and see people, to meet friends, to go to openings, to dinner, without having to drive over 60 miles. I wish my studio were closer to, or in, an urban environment. I would love to walk out of my studio and get a coffee. I suppose I can do that now, but I have to make the coffee myself.What is your favorite local museum?I love going to Site Santa Fe, though it is almost 70 miles away, so not super local. Also in Santa Fe, I love the IAIA Museum of Contemporary Native Arts. I always get charged up by the exhibitions there. New Mexico has many really interesting museums that all require long drives; some really surprised me, including the Bradbury Science Museum in Los Alamos, the telephone museum in Albuquerque, and the Roswell UFO Museum. That one was really fun.What is your favorite art material to work with?Paper! Absolutely paper; I print it; relief, intaglio, and lithography. I marble it, using suminagashi technique. I cut it up and weave it. I make boats and books with paper. I love paper, and the primary artwork I collect is also on paper.
                  
                      
                        Community
                      
                      
                        A View From the Easel

title: What I Got Wrong About Krasner and Pollock
description:
Opinion
                I had assumed that loving an artist meant disappearing a little, and I had assumed that Lee Krasner had
body:
Opinion
                I had assumed that loving an artist meant disappearing a little, and I had assumed that Lee Krasner had been forced to shrink, too.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Lia Strasser's drawings inspired by a visit to the Pollock-Krasner House (artwork © Lia Strasser)
    
        
            Earlier this year, the Metropolitan Museum of Art announced its forthcoming exhibition Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous on Instagram, alongside a photograph of the artists by Hans Namuth. Seething, I looked to the comments for affirmation. I didn't have to scroll for long. "Give her a solo show!"Months earlier, I had visited the Pollock-Krasner House in Springs, East Hampton, knowing far more about Jackson Pollock than I did Lee Krasner. I am a painter myself, and I had come to Springs in the wreck of yet another failed relationship … with a painter. I thought I already knew Krasner's story. I thought her story was partly my own.The first stop on the tour was Krasner's studio: a small second-floor bedroom overlooking Accabonac Creek. The guide told us Pollock would displace Krasner when it was too cold to paint in the barn, and how she would then work by the warmth of the kitchen stove: a woman in the kitchen in the 1950s, working around her husband's tempestuousness. In the living room, we learned how Krasner navigated gender bias, poverty, and Pollock's alcoholism while using her own credibility in the art world to promote his paintings, the sales of which supported their frugal life. I mourned all the paintings that could have been had she not been saddled with such a mess.Lee Krasner, Jackson Pollock, and visitors in the studio in East Hampton, New York, August 23, 1953 (photo Tony Vaccaro/Getty Images)Then we crossed the lawn to the barn and its famous floor, where Pollock developed his drip technique. But I stared instead at the bare rectangles on the walls, fringed with splattered paint, the spaces where Krasner's canvases had hung. After Pollock's death, it took her a year to claim the studio. When she finally did, she painted at a sweeping scale and filled the barn with her own explosive work. As the guide described Krasner's grief-induced insomnia, I couldn't reconcile it: Why, when she finally had the studio her spirit and ambition deserved, when she was rid of the weight of that difficult man, was she so bereft?The tour ended, and I grumbled my way into the gift shop. Still looking for an injustice to protest, I struck up a conversation with an employee about women painters. He placed a large yellow book in my hands, saying, "This is a wonderful introduction, not just to Lee, but to the other women of Abstract Expressionism." Only then did he introduce himself: Matthew Ward, director of the Pollock-Krasner House. I bought Mary Gabriel's Ninth Street Women (2018), and we said goodbye. I stared at the bare rectangles on the walls, fringed with splattered paint, the spaces where Krasner's canvases had hung. (artwork © Lia Strasser)In the following months, I made a series of drawings from my photographs of the house and finished Gabriel's book. I sent Matt a short video of the work, and he suggested we discuss it over a call. About a week before we spoke, The Met announced the show. I assumed Matt would commiserate with me over the decision to exhibit Krasner alongside Pollock, but he was excited."A lot of people don't know this, but for two of the most avant-garde artists of their time, they led surprisingly domestic lives,” he told me. “They slept in separate beds, and they made appointments to visit each other's studios. The romance was in the passion for their art, in what the other was doing on canvas."Throughout our conversation, I was struck by how often Matt said "they" and "them." He rarely referred to one artist apart from the other. Every time I tried to steer him toward Krasner's sacrifices, he returned to their partnership. "He was the face of their business, but she managed everything. I'm not sure Jackson would have kept painting if it weren't for Lee."Then he offered a thought that astonished me. He described Krasner's habit of destroying and reassembling older paintings that no longer felt true to the artist she had become, and wondered whether she had done something similar with her memories of Pollock. She outlived him by almost three decades. Perhaps she had revised the relationship to align with the Lee Krasner she became.The guide told us Pollock would displace Krasner when it was too cold to paint in the barn, and how she would then work by the warmth of the kitchen stove. (artwork © Lia Strasser)Still, I couldn't imagine anyone who knew Krasner's life intimately thinking The Met's decision was right. When I googled "contact Mary Gabriel," the most promising result was an author page on her publisher's website. I sent my note into the void and began working on a backup plan. Four days later, the author agreed to a Zoom call from her home in Ireland.

title: The Art World Reacts to Yayoi Kusama’s Passing
description:

body:
News
                Artists, designers, galleries, and museums have shared homages to the legacy of the pop icon, who died on August 14.  
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            Celebrity Illustrator Mr Doodle drew over a photo of Yayoi Kusama in his signature style. (image courtesy Mr Doodle)From her beloved dotted pumpkins to her immersive Infinity Mirror Rooms, artist Yayoi Kusama reenvisioned the pop avant-garde with artworks that often doubled as social commentary and public protest. Following this week's news of her passing at the age of 97, artists, galleries, museums, and fashion houses around the world have taken to social media to reflect on the seismic loss. Tributes from Louis Vuitton to professional doodlers have flooded Instagram, each remembering the artist as a daring, radical, and complex force. Across generations and disciplines, these 12 testimonies cement Kusama’s legacy in polka-dotted perpetuity. Glenn Scott WrightReflecting on decades of friendship, teatime, and routine visits with the late artist, Glenn Scott Wright, president of the Victoria Miro Gallery, writes, “Spending time with Kusama will forever be one of the greatest privileges of my life, and her wisdom, humour and friendship will be a part of my own eternal soul.”Screenshot Hyperallergic via InstagramDean SameshimaThrough old photographs of Kusama’s 1998 performance at the Chateau Marmont in West Hollywood, Dean Sameshima recounts witnessing the artist’s thrilling, “tense” performance. Kusama would collect signature dots from audience members in this untitled number and stick them onto her fellow performers. Screenshot Hyperallergic via InstagramKaty Hessel/The Great Women ArtistsBritish art historian Katy Hessel traces Kusama’s breaking from convention, captured in the small but mighty dot. “She showed us that all of those dots matter,” Hessel writes. “It takes every single one of them to light up in order to make up the cosmos, to make something beautiful; it requires us to work together.”Screenshot Hyperallergic via InstagramMuseum LudwigThe Museum Ludwig in Cologne concluded a major retrospective of Kusama’s work on August 2, just 12 days before the artist passed away. Over 480,000 people visited the five-month-long exhibition, the most successful in the institution’s history, according to David Zwirner gallery.Screenshot Hyperallergic via InstagramSondra MeszarosCalgary-based artist Sondra Meszaros pays homage to Kusama’s recurring philosophy of “Love Forever,” a phrase that would undergird dozens of the artist’s creations. Kusama routinely spread the love, passing out badges with the slogan to audience members at a 2012 exhibition at the Whitney Museum of American Art. Screenshot Hyperallergic via InstagramLouisiana ChannelThe Louisiana Museum of Art’s video channel posted images of one of its founding editors, Christian Lund, greeting Kusama at eye level. The Louisiana Channel’s next newsletter will detail that exchange from Lund’s perspective, brief, powerful, and memorable as it was. Screenshot Hyperallergic via InstagramDavid Zwirner“At the time of her passing, Kusama was, without a doubt, the most famous living artist in the world,” writes David Zwirner, who represented the artist since 2013. Kusama had six solo exhibitions at Zwirner’s gallery, the latest being Yayoi Kusama: I Spend Each Day Embracing Flowers in 2023, which drew lines down the block to experience one of her Infinity Rooms.Screenshot Hyperallergic via Instagram
